claim: The telencephalon and eye in mammals are originated from adjacent fields at the anterior neural plate.
source: The telencephalon and eye in mammals are originated from adjacent fields at the anterior neural plate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction, drawing from established scientific knowledge about mammalian development.

claim: Morphogenesis of these fields generates telencephalon, optic-stalk, optic-disc, and neuroretina along a spatial axis.
source: Morphogenesis of these fields generates telencephalon, optic-stalk, optic-disc, and neuroretina along a spatial axis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract, drawing from established knowledge of developmental biology.

claim: Human telencephalon-eye organoids comprise concentric zones of telencephalic, optic-stalk, optic-disc, and neuroretinal tissues along the center-periphery axis.
source: Here, we report self-formation of human telencephalon-eye organoids comprising concentric zones of telencephalic, optic-stalk, optic-disc, and neuroretinal tissues along the center-periphery axis.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Initially-differentiated RGCs grew axons towards and then along a path defined by adjacent PAX2+ VSX2+ optic-disc cells.
source: Initially-differentiated RGCs grew axons towards and then along a path defined by adjacent PAX2+ VSX2+ optic-disc cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing of these organoids confirmed telencephalic and ocular identities.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing of these organoids not only confirmed telencephalic and ocular identities but also identified expression signatures of early optic-disc, optic-stalk, and RGCs.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified expression signatures of early optic-disc, optic-stalk, and RGCs.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing of these organoids not only confirmed telencephalic and ocular identities but also identified expression signatures of early optic-disc, optic-stalk, and RGCs.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Expression signatures in CONCEPT organoids were similar to those in human fetal retinas.
source: These signatures were similar to those in human fetal retinas.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Optic-disc cells in these organoids differentially expressed FGF8 and FGF9.
source: Optic-disc cells in these organoids differentially expressed FGF8 and FGF9
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data in Figure 4 and in situ hybridization in Figure 9.

claim: FGFR inhibitions drastically decreased early RGC differentiation and directional axon growth.
source: FGFR inhibitions drastically decreased early RGC differentiation and directional axon growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 using FGFR inhibitor PD 161570.

claim: CNTN2 is a RGC-specific cell-surface marker.
source: Through the RGC-specific cell-surface marker CNTN2 identified here, electrophysiologically excitable RGCs were isolated under a native condition.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data in Figure 4 and immunostaining in Figure 7.

claim: Electrophysiologically excitable RGCs were isolated under a native condition using CNTN2.
source: Through the RGC-specific cell-surface marker CNTN2 identified here, electrophysiologically excitable RGCs were isolated under a native condition.
evidence: This is supported by MACS isolation data in Figure 7 and electrophysiology data in Figure 8.

claim: In mice, fate mapping of the anterior neural plate reveals that the eye field is in rostral regions surrounded anteriorly and laterally by the telencephalic field and caudally and medially by the hypothalamic field.
source: In mice, fate mapping of the anterior neural plate reveals that the eye field is in rostral regions surrounded anteriorly and laterally by the telencephalic field and caudally and medially by the hypothalamic field, indicating the proximity of their embryonic origins (Inoue et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2000.

claim: Evagination of the eye field generates bilateral optic vesicles and optic stalks.
source: Subsequent evagination of the eye field generates bilateral optic vesicles and optic stalks, and the optic stalk connects the optic vesicle to the forebrain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of eye development.

claim: The optic vesicle invaginates ventrally, resulting in the formation of the double-layered optic cup.
source: The optic vesicle then invaginates ventrally, resulting in the formation of the double-layered optic cup in which the inner and outer layers develop into the neuroretina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), respectively.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of eye development.

claim: The inner and outer layers of the optic cup develop into the neuroretina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), respectively.
source: The optic vesicle then invaginates ventrally, resulting in the formation of the double-layered optic cup in which the inner and outer layers develop into the neuroretina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), respectively.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of eye development.

claim: The posterior pole of the optic cup forms the optic disc.
source: The posterior pole of the optic cup forms the optic disc (also known as optic nerve head).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of eye development.

claim: In the central neuroretina close to the nascent optic disc, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) start to appear as the optic fissure nearly closes.
source: In the central neuroretina close to the nascent optic disc, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) start to appear as the optic fissure nearly closes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of retinal development.

claim: Early RGC axons find their path toward the optic disc and then enter the optic stalk to reach the brain.
source: Early RGC axons find their path toward the optic disc and then enter the optic stalk to reach the brain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of RGC axon pathfinding.

claim: Concentrically organized growth-promoting and growth-inhibitory guidance cues around the optic disc regulate RGC axon growth and pathfinding through multiple mechanisms.
source: Concentrically organized growth-promoting and growth-inhibitory guidance cues around the optic disc regulate RGC axon growth and pathfinding through multiple mechanisms (Erskine and Herrera, 2007; Erskine and Herrera, 2014; Oster et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erskine and Herrera, 2007; Erskine and Herrera, 2014; Oster et al., 2004.

claim: In mice, Foxg1 is specifically expressed in the presumptive telencephalon and is essential for the development of the cerebral hemispheres.
source: In mice, Foxg1 is specifically expressed in the presumptive telencephalon and is essential for the development of the cerebral hemispheres (Xuan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xuan et al., 1995.

claim: Pax6 is specifically expressed in the eye field and is essential for the development of multiple ocular tissues, such as the neuroretina, lens, and RPE.
source: Pax6 is specifically expressed in the eye field and is essential for the development of multiple ocular tissues, such as the neuroretina, lens, and RPE (Ashery-Padan et al., 2000; Bäumer et al., 2003; Marquardt et al., 2001; Zuber et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ashery-Padan et al., 2000; Bäumer et al., 2003; Marquardt et al., 2001; Zuber et al., 2003.

claim: Vsx2 and Mitf are specifically expressed in the neuroretina and RPE, respectively, and are essential for retinal development.
source: Vsx2 and Mitf are specifically expressed in the neuroretina and RPE, respectively, and are essential for retinal development (Bharti et al., 2012; Horsford et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2010; Rowan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bharti et al., 2012; Horsford et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2010; Rowan et al., 2004.

claim: Pax2 is expressed in the optic stalk, optic vesicles, central neuroretina, and optic disc.
source: Pax2 is expressed in the optic stalk, optic vesicles, central neuroretina, and optic disc; Pax2 is essential for optic stalk and nerve development (Macdonald et al., 1997; Martinez-Morales et al., 2001; Schwarz et al., 2000; Torres et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Macdonald et al., 1997; Martinez-Morales et al., 2001; Schwarz et al., 2000; Torres et al., 1996.

claim: Pax2 is essential for optic stalk and nerve development.
source: Pax2 is expressed in the optic stalk, optic vesicles, central neuroretina, and optic disc; Pax2 is essential for optic stalk and nerve development (Macdonald et al., 1997; Martinez-Morales et al., 2001; Schwarz et al., 2000; Torres et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Macdonald et al., 1997; Martinez-Morales et al., 2001; Schwarz et al., 2000; Torres et al., 1996.

claim: Fgf8 is specifically expressed at the rostral forebrain at early stages and induces Foxg1 expression.
source: Fgf8 is specifically expressed at the rostral forebrain at early stages, induces Foxg1 expression (Shimamura and Rubenstein, 1997), and regulates telencephalic patterning in a dose-dependent manner (Storm et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shimamura and Rubenstein, 1997; Storm et al., 2006.

claim: Fgf8 regulates telencephalic patterning in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Fgf8 is specifically expressed at the rostral forebrain at early stages, induces Foxg1 expression (Shimamura and Rubenstein, 1997), and regulates telencephalic patterning in a dose-dependent manner (Storm et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Storm et al., 2006.

claim: Fgf8 maintains Pax2 expression in the optic stalk.
source: Fgf8 also maintains Pax2 expression in the optic stalk (Soukkarieh et al., 2007), and Fgf8 and Fgf3 coordinate the initiation of retinal differentiation in chicks (Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Vogel-Höpker et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soukkarieh et al., 2007.

claim: Fgf8 and Fgf3 coordinate the initiation of retinal differentiation in chicks.
source: Fgf8 also maintains Pax2 expression in the optic stalk (Soukkarieh et al., 2007), and Fgf8 and Fgf3 coordinate the initiation of retinal differentiation in chicks (Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Vogel-Höpker et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Vogel-Höpker et al., 2000.

claim: Cysts are hollow spheres of a columnar epithelium that is induced from human pluripotent stem cells via embedding hESC sheets in Matrigel.
source: Cysts are hollow spheres of a columnar epithelium that is induced from human pluripotent stem cells via embedding hESC sheets in Matrigel; they are used to generate retinal cells (Kim et al., 2019; Lowe et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2019; Lowe et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: The epithelial structure of cysts was demonstrated by apical localization of the TJP1::GFP reporter at the lumen.
source: The epithelial structure of cysts was demonstrated by apical localization of the TJP1::GFP reporter at the lumen (Figure 1C), consistent with previous findings (Lowe et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Lowe et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: In mice, Foxg1 was specifically expressed in the E10 telencephalon at high levels.
source: In mice, Foxg1 was specifically expressed in the E10 telencephalon at high levels; it was also expressed in the optic stalk, invaginating optic cup, and lens at lower levels, with the rostral optic stalk connecting the telencephalic vesicle to the invaginating optic cup (Figure 1E; Xuan et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Xuan et al., 1995.

claim: Foxg1 was also expressed in the optic stalk, invaginating optic cup, and lens at lower levels in E10 mice.
source: In mice, Foxg1 was specifically expressed in the E10 telencephalon at high levels; it was also expressed in the optic stalk, invaginating optic cup, and lens at lower levels, with the rostral optic stalk connecting the telencephalic vesicle to the invaginating optic cup (Figure 1E; Xuan et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Xuan et al., 1995.

claim: Vsx2 was specifically expressed in the E10 neuroretina in mice.
source: Vsx2 was specifically expressed in the E10 neuroretina (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Pax6 was specifically expressed in the E10.5 neuroretina, RPE, lens vesicles, and surface ectoderm in mice.
source: Pax6 was specifically expressed in the E10.5 neuroretina, RPE, lens vesicles, and surface ectoderm (Figure 1G; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G and citation to Liu et al., 2010.

claim: In CONCEPT structures, the expression of FOXG1, VSX2, and PAX6 generally exhibited concentric patterns spanning from the center to the periphery at days 15–17.
source: In CONCEPT structures, the expression of FOXG1, VSX2, and PAX6 generally exhibited concentric patterns spanning from the center to the periphery at days 15–17 (Figure 1H–K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; a scheme in the left panel in B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H-K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At day 17, PAX6 was expressed in multiple concentric zones at distinct levels, with a higher level at a circular zone that also expressed VSX2.
source: At this stage, PAX6 was expressed in multiple concentric zones at distinct levels, with a higher level at a circular zone that also expressed VSX2 (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At day 26, VSX2 expression expanded peripherally compared to its expression at day 17.
source: At day 26, VSX2 expression expanded peripherally compared to its expression at day 17 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and largely overlapped with PAX6 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids, FGF8, BMP4, and BMP7 were expressed in attached cell colonies starting from early stages.
source: In CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids, FGF8, BMP4, and BMP7 were expressed in attached cell colonies starting from early stages (Figure 1P, S and T) and subsequently exhibited circular patterns.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1P, S and T.

claim: At day 10, the expression of BMP4 and BMP7 delineated multiple rings, with a big ring mostly at the center surrounded by numerous small rings.
source: At day 10, the expression of BMP4 and BMP7 delineated multiple rings, with a big ring mostly at the center surrounded by numerous small rings (Figure 1P and S).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1P and S.

claim: At day 17, circular expression patterns of BMP4 and FGF8 emerged.
source: At day 17, circular expression patterns of BMP4 and FGF8 emerged (Figure 1Q and U).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1Q and U.

claim: At day 25, BMP4, FGF8, and BMP7 expression clearly marked circular zones.
source: At day 25, BMP4, FGF8, and BMP7 expression clearly marked circular zones (Figure 1R, V, W).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1R, V, W.

claim: In mice, transcription factor Pou4f2 is expressed in the early differentiated RGCs and required for the development of a large set of RGCs.
source: In mice, transcription factor Pou4f2 is expressed in the early differentiated RGCs and required for the development of a large set of RGCs (Gan et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gan et al., 1996.

claim: Tubb3 is expressed in the somas and axons of differentiating RGCs.
source: Tubb3 is expressed in the somas and axons of differentiating RGCs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of RGC markers.

claim: In CONCEPT organoids, POU4F2 and TUBB3 were detectable as early as day 17 and increased to higher levels at day 22.
source: In CONCEPT organoids, POU4F2 and TUBB3 were detectable as early as day 17 and increased to higher levels at day 22.
evidence: This is based on observations from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RGCs grew directional long axons that followed a circular path.
source: Interestingly, RGCs grew directional long axons that followed a circular path (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The circular path of RGC axon outgrowth became more evident in organoids at day 26.
source: The circular path of RGC axon outgrowth became more evident in organoids at day 26 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Presumptive optic disc cells expressed VSX2, whereas optic stalk cells did not.
source: Additionally, presumptive optic disc cells expressed VSX2, whereas optic stalk cells did not (Figure 1F, Figure 2E; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F, Figure 2E and citation to Liu et al., 2010.

claim: In CONCEPT organoids, there were two PAX2+ cell populations that formed two adjacent rings.
source: In CONCEPT organoids, there were two PAX2+ cell populations that formed two adjacent rings (Figure 2H–L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H-L.

claim: POU4F2+ RGCs grew TUBB3+ axons toward and then navigated along the adjacent PAX2+ VSX2+ cell population.
source: POU4F2+ RGCs grew TUBB3+ axons toward and then navigated along the adjacent PAX2+ VSX2+ cell population (Figure 2H–L), mimicking axon growth from the nascent RGCs toward the optic disc in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H-L.

claim: The PAX2+ VSX2- cell population at the inner zone set up an inner boundary of the path for RGC axon growth.
source: Meanwhile, the PAX2+ VSX2- cell population at the inner zone set up an inner boundary of the path for RGC axon growth, mimicking the optic stalk that spatially confines RGC axon growth in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial organization described and shown in Figure 2H-L.

claim: CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids at around day 25 contained transparent structures reminiscent of the ocular lens.
source: CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids at around day 25 contained transparent structures reminiscent of the ocular lens.
evidence: This is based on observations from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Starting at day 22, lens markers CRYAA and beta crystallin (CRY B) were found.
source: Starting at day 22, lens markers CRYAA and beta crystallin (CRY B) were found (Figure 3A and B) and continuously expressed in these transparent cell structures (Figure 3C, D and K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, B, C, D and K.

claim: These transparent structures were not stained by DAPI, indicating denucleation in these lens cells.
source: Interestingly, these transparent structures were not stained by DAPI (Figure 3C–F), indicating denucleation in these lens cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C-F and inference from the lack of DAPI staining.

claim: When CONCEPT organoids were detached using Dispase at around day 28 and continuously grown as suspension cultures, crystal-like clusters with fused transparent spheres—lentoid bodies—were found.
source: When CONCEPT organoids were detached using Dispase at around day 28 and continuously grown as suspension cultures, crystal-like clusters with fused transparent spheres—lentoid bodies—were found, and they continuously survived for months (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Lentoid bodies highly expressed gamma crystallin (CRY G).
source: Lentoid bodies highly expressed gamma crystallin (CRY G; Figure 3L), confirming their lens identity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: In mice, terminally differentiated lens fiber cells are free of organelles and featured by specialized interlocking cell membrane domains shown as ball-and-sockets and protrusions.
source: In mice, terminally differentiated lens fiber cells are free of organelles and featured by specialized interlocking cell membrane domains shown as ball-and-sockets and protrusions (Biswas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Biswas et al., 2010.

claim: Lentoid bodies were free of organelles and exhibited ball-and-socket structures.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy, we found that our lentoid bodies were free of organelles and exhibited ball-and-socket structures (Figure 3M and N).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3M and N.

claim: Cell Ranger mapping showed that 11158 single cells were sequenced at a depth of 27,842 reads and 2967 genes per cell.
source: Cell Ranger mapping showed that 11158 single cells were sequenced at a depth of 27,842 reads and 2967 genes per cell, and the dataset were further analyzed using Seurat (v3.2.0) (Stuart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis and citation to Stuart et al., 2019.

claim: Cell filtration resulted in 10,218 cells.
source: Cell filtration (nFeature_RNA >200 & nFeature_RNA <6000 & percent.mt <20) resulted in 10,218 cells.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Cell clustering grouped cells into 14 clusters.
source: Cell clustering grouped cells into 14 clusters (Figure 4A; Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: CONCEPT organoids at day 24 were mostly composed of FOXG1+ telencephalic cells and PAX6+ and/or VSX2+ retinal cells.
source: CONCEPT organoids at day 24 were mostly composed of FOXG1+ telencephalic cells (clusters 10, 3, 12, 1, 4, 8, 9, 13) and PAX6+ and/or VSX2+ retinal cells (clusters 2, 7, 5, 6, 11; Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-E.

claim: Diencephalon markers (GBX2, WNT3, SOX14) and midbrain/hindbrain markers (EN2, PAX7, TFAP2B) were rarely expressed in CONCEPT organoids.
source: In contrast to telencephalon and retinal markers, diencephalon markers (GBX2, WNT3, SOX14; Chatterjee and Li, 2012; Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012) and midbrain/hindbrain markers (EN2, PAX7, TFAP2B; Yao et al., 2017) were rarely expressed (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citations to Chatterjee and Li, 2012; Martinez-Ferre and Martinez, 2012; Yao et al., 2017.

claim: Top DEGs in clusters 4, 8, 9, 1 included SOX3, FGFR2, PRRX1, and EDNRB, which mouse orthologs are specifically expressed in the dorsal telencephalon.
source: Top DEGs in clusters 4, 8, 9, 1 included SOX3, FGFR2, PRRX1, and EDNRB (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–D), which mouse orthologs are specifically expressed in the dorsal telencephalon (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 5B-E.

claim: Top DEGs in clusters 12, 3, 10 included DLX2, DLX6-AS1, DLX1, and RGS16, which mouse orthologs are specifically expressed in the ventral telencephalon.
source: Top DEGs in clusters 12, 3, 10 included DLX2, DLX6-AS1, DLX1, and RGS16 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E–H), which mouse orthologs are specifically expressed in the ventral telencephalon (Figure 4—figure supplement 5F–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 5F-I.

claim: Telencephalic cells in CONCEPT organoids at day 24 comprise both dorsal and ventral telencephalic cells.
source: Therefore, telencephalic cells in CONCEPT organoids at day 24 comprise both dorsal and ventral telencephalic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of dorsal and ventral telencephalic markers.

claim: Cluster 6 differentially expressed RPE markers, e.g., PMEL, HSD17B2, DCT, and MITF, indicating they were mostly differentiating RPE cells.
source: Cluster 6 differentially expressed RPE markers, e.g., PMEL, HSD17B2, DCT, and MITF (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), indicating they were mostly differentiating RPE cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6 and inference from marker expression.

claim: PAX2 was mostly expressed in cluster 2 and subsets of clusters 7, 5, 0, 4, 8, and 9.
source: PAX2 was mostly expressed in cluster 2 and subsets of clusters 7, 5, 0, 4, 8, and 9 (Figure 4A and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and F.

claim: PAX2+ VSX2+ cells in cluster 2 and subsets of clusters 7, 5, and 0 were assigned as optic disc (OD) cells.
source: Since clusters 2, 7, 5, and 0 expressed VSX2 (Figure 4E and F), we deduced that PAX2+ VSX2+ cells in cluster 2 and subsets of clusters 7, 5, and 0 corresponded to those PAX2+ VSX2+ cells that defined the path for RGC axon growth (Figure 2H–L) and therefore were assigned as optic disc (OD) cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-expression of PAX2 and VSX2 and their spatial organization shown in Figure 2H-L.

claim: COL9A3 and COL13A1 were differentially expressed in cluster 2.
source: Interestingly, COL9A3 and COL13A1 were differentially expressed in cluster 2 (Figure 4G and H; Figure 4—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4G, H and Figure 4—figure supplement 7A.

claim: COL13A1 is prominently expressed in the optic disc of human fetal retinas.
source: Previous in situ hybridization results indicate that COL13A1 is prominently expressed in the optic disc of human fetal retinas (Sandberg-Lall et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sandberg-Lall et al., 2000.

claim: Cluster 2 also differentially expressed glaucoma gene CYP1B1, morphogen-encoding genes LEFTY2, FGF9, and FGF8.
source: Cluster 2 also differentially expressed glaucoma gene CYP1B1, morphogen-encoding genes LEFTY2, FGF9, and FGF8 (Figure 4I–L; Figure 4—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4I-L and Figure 4—figure supplement 7A.

claim: PAX2+ VSX2- cells were at edges of telencephalic clusters 4, 8, 9 and expressed the optic stalk marker VAX1.
source: In contrast to assigned optic disc cells, PAX2+ VSX2- cells were at edges of telencephalic clusters 4, 8, 9 (Figure 4A, E and F) and expressed the optic stalk marker VAX1 (Figure 4F and M).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, E, F and M.

claim: PAX2+ VSX2- cells in subsets of clusters 4, 8, 9 were assigned as optic stalk cells (OS).
source: Therefore, PAX2+ VSX2- cells in subsets of clusters 4, 8, 9 were assigned as optic stalk cells (OS; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of PAX2 without VSX2 and expression of optic stalk marker VAX1.

claim: PAX2+ VSX2- optic stalk cells also differentially expressed CNTNAP2, ALDHA3, and LAMP5, which mouse orthologs are expressed in the optic stalk/nerve.
source: PAX2+ VSX2- optic stalk cells also differentially expressed CNTNAP2, ALDHA3, and LAMP5 (Figure 4N–P), which mouse orthologs are expressed in the optic stalk/nerve (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4N-P and Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: Cluster 11 differentially expressed neurogenic retinal progenitor marker ATOH7.
source: Interestingly, cluster 11 differentially expressed neurogenic retinal progenitor marker ATOH7 (Figure 4Q), indicating that these cells underwent retinal differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4Q and inference from marker expression.

claim: A large portion of cluster 11 differentially expressed POU4F2, indicating their RGC identity.
source: A large portion of cluster 11 differentially expressed POU4F2 (Figure 4R), indicating their RGC identity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4R and inference from marker expression.

claim: CNTN2 was largely co-expressed with POU4F2 in cluster 11.
source: Notably, CNTN2, which encodes a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored cell membrane protein, was largely co-expressed with POU4F2 (Figure 4R and S).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4R and S.

claim: Cluster 11 also differentially expressed RGC marker SNCG.
source: Cluster 11 also differentially expressed RGC marker SNCG (Figure 4T).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4T.

claim: Two small portions of cluster 11 differentially expressed photoreceptor markers OTX2 and CRX and amacrine/horizontal cell markers TFAP2C and PTF1A, respectively.
source: Two small portions of cluster 11 differentially expressed photoreceptor markers OTX2 and CRX (Figure 4U and V) and amacrine/horizontal cell markers TFAP2C and PTF1A (Figure 4W–X), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4U, V, W and X.

claim: Cluster 11 comprises differentiating retinal neurons, predominantly early RGCs.
source: Therefore, cluster 11 comprises differentiating retinal neurons, predominantly early RGCs
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of neurogenic and RGC markers.

claim: Cell surface protein gene CNTN2 is differentially expressed in early RGCs.
source: cell surface protein gene CNTN2 is differentially expressed in early RGCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-expression of CNTN2 with POU4F2 in cluster 11.

claim: PAX2+ cells were extremely rare in Gabriel et al.'s organoids; there were only eight and five PAX2+ cells scattering across Gabriel et al.'s datasets at day 30 and day 60, respectively.
source: Interestingly, PAX2+ cells were extremely rare; there were only eight and five PAX2+ cells scattering across Gabriel et al.'s datasets at day 30 and day 60, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 10B, D), indicating that Gabriel et al.'s organoids do not have PAX2+ cell clusters that were found in CONCEPT organoids.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Gabriel et al.'s dataset shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 10B, D.

claim: In Gabriel et al.'s organoids on day 30, FOXG1+ telencephalic progenitors, SIX3+ neuroretinal progenitors, and ATOH7+ neurogenic progenitors were extremely rare.
source: In Gabriel et al.'s organoids on day 30, FOXG1+ telencephalic progenitors, SIX3+ neuroretinal progenitors, and ATOH7+ neurogenic progenitors were extremely rare (Figure 4—figure supplement 10E–G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Gabriel et al.'s dataset shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 10E-G.

claim: PAX2+ optic disc/stalk, FOXG1+ telencephalic, and VSX2+ neuroretinal cell clusters that were found in CONCEPT organoids did not exist in Gabriel et al.'s organoids.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that PAX2+ optic disc/stalk, FOXG1+ telencephalic, and VSX2+ neuroretinal cell clusters that were found in CONCEPT organoids did not exist in Gabriel et al.'s organoids, indicating striking differences between Gabriel et al.'s organoids and our CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative analysis of the two datasets.

claim: CONCEPT organoids and human fetal retinas had similar expression signatures.
source: Transcriptomic comparisons between CONCEPT organoids at day 24 and human fetal retinas at HWG9 (Lu et al., 2020) indicate that CONCEPT organoids and human fetal retinas had similar expression signatures.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 5 and citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: Cluster 18 in HGW9 retinas differentially expressed PAX2, COL9A3, CYP1B1, SEMA5A, and FGF9, which were top DEGs of cluster 2 in CONCEPT organoids.
source: Notably, cluster 18 differentially expressed PAX2, COL9A3, CYP1B1, SEMA5A, and FGF9 (Figure 5B–F), which were top DEGs of cluster 2 in CONCEPT organoids (Figure 4F, G, I and K; Figure 4—figure supplement 9A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-F and Figure 4F, G, I, K.

claim: 64/113 DEGs of cluster 18 in HGW9 were also DEGs of cluster 2 in CONCEPT organoids.
source: Overall, 64/113 DEGs of cluster 18 in HGW9 were also DEGs of cluster 2 in CONCEPT organoids.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of DEGs.

claim: In both HGW9 and CONCEPT organoids, expression of OLIG2, CD44, and GFAP was undetectable, indicating that astrocytes had not been generated yet at these stages.
source: In both HGW9 and CONCEPT organoids, expression of OLIG2, CD44, and GFAP was undetectable (Figure 4—figure supplement 11), indicating that astrocytes had not been generated yet at these stages.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 11 and inference from lack of astrocyte marker expression.

claim: CNTN2 was also largely co-expressed with POU4F2 in human fetal RGCs.
source: Notably, CNTN2 was also largely co-expressed with POU4F2 in human fetal RGCs (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5L and M.

claim: When cells in cluster 18 from HGW9 were combined with cells in clusters 2, 4, 5, 7 from CONCEPT organoids for Seurat anchor-based clustering, cells in cluster 18 from HGW9 (H18) were grouped with cluster 2 from CONCEPT organoids (C2, assigned optic disc).
source: When cells in cluster 18 and retinal progenitor clusters from the HGW9 dataset were combined with cells in clusters 2, 4, 5, 7 from the CONCEPT dataset for Seurat anchor-based clustering, cells in cluster 18 from HGW9 (H18) were grouped with cluster 2 from CONCEPT organoids (C2, assigned optic disc; N), and these cells expressed both PAX2 and VSX2 (arrowheads in Figure 5N–R).
evidence: This is supported by integrated clustering analysis shown in Figure 5N-R.

claim: A small portion of H18 cells were grouped with cluster 4 from CONCEPT organoids (C4, assigned optic stalk), and these cells expressed PAX2 but not VSX2.
source: A small portion of H18 cells were grouped with cluster 4 from CONCEPT organoids (C4, assigned optic stalk; N), and these cells expressed PAX2 but not VSX2 (arrows in Figure 5N–R).
evidence: This is supported by integrated clustering analysis shown in Figure 5N-R.

claim: Most of PAX2+ cells from the HGW9 dataset are optic disc cells, whereas a small portion are optic stalk cells.
source: These findings indicate that most of PAX2+ cells from the HGW9 dataset are optic disc cells, whereas a small portion are optic stalk cells, which is consistent with the expectation that optic disc cells are preserved whereas optic stalk cells are mostly lost in whole retina preparations.
evidence: This is inferred from the integrated clustering analysis and knowledge about tissue preparation.

claim: Human fetal retinas HGW9 were at a more advanced stage than CONCEPT organoids.
source: We would like to point out that human fetal retinas HGW9 were at a more advanced stage than CONCEPT organoids, as indicated by the counts of days and the proportion of RGCs (Figure 5L and M; Figure 4R and S).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of developmental stages and RGC proportions shown in Figure 5L, M and Figure 4R, S.

claim: For DEGs of cluster 2 in CONCEPT organoids, top enriched GO terms in GO:MF, GO:CC, and GO:BP were extracellular matrix structural constituent, collagen-containing extracellular matrix, and system development, respectively.
source: For DEGs of cluster 2 in CONCEPT organoids, top enriched GO terms in GO:MF, GO:CC, and GO:BP were extracellular matrix structural constituent, collagen-containing extracellular matrix, and system development, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: For DEGs of cluster 18 in human fetal retinas HGW9, top enriched GO terms in GO:MF, GO:CC, and GO:BP were cell adhesion molecule binding, extracellular space, and developmental process, respectively.
source: For DEGs of cluster 18 in human fetal retinas HGW9, top enriched GO terms in GO:MF, GO:CC, and GO:BP were cell adhesion molecule binding, extracellular space, and developmental process, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Many GO terms were enriched in both samples, further indicating transcriptomic similarities in PAX2+ optic disc cells between CONCEPT organoids and human fetal retinas.
source: Many GO terms were enriched in both samples, further indicating transcriptomic similarities in PAX2+ optic disc cells between CONCEPT organoids and human fetal retinas.
evidence: This is inferred from the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: In literature, Cntn2 is specifically expressed in developing RGCs in mice and chicks.
source: In literature, Cntn2 is specifically expressed in developing RGCs in mice and chicks (Chatzopoulou et al., 2008; Yamagata and Sanes, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chatzopoulou et al., 2008; Yamagata and Sanes, 2012.

claim: In CONCEPT at day 25, CNTN2 exhibited an expression pattern very similar to that of TUBB3.
source: In CONCEPT at day 25, CNTN2 exhibited an expression pattern very similar to that of TUBB3 (Figure 2, Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 7.

claim: CNTN2 was found in the cell membrane of RGCs that expressed POU4F2 in the cell nucleus.
source: CNTN2 was found in the cell membrane of RGCs that expressed POU4F2 in the cell nucleus (Figure 7A, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, D.

claim: PAX2+ cells formed inner and outer concentric zones, which were designated as optic-stalk and optic-disc cells, respectively.
source: PAX2+ cells formed inner and outer concentric zones, which were designated as optic-stalk and optic-disc cells, respectively.
evidence: This is based on spatial organization and marker expression patterns.

claim: POU4F2+ RGCs formed a dense circular zone adjacent to PAX2+ optic disc cells; POU4F2+ RGCs were sparse in more peripheral areas.
source: POU4F2+ RGCs formed a dense circular zone adjacent to PAX2+ optic disc cells; POU4F2+ RGCs were sparse in more peripheral areas (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Early differentiated RGCs were adjacent to PAX2+ optic disc cells.
source: These findings indicate that early differentiated RGCs were adjacent to PAX2+ optic disc cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial organization shown in Figure 7.

claim: RGCs in the dense POU4F2+ zone grew CNTN2+ axons toward and then along the path defined by adjacent PAX2+ optic disc cells.
source: Interestingly, RGCs in the dense POU4F2+ zone grew CNTN2+ axons toward and then along the path defined by adjacent PAX2+ optic disc cells (Figure 7A–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: In areas where there was a gap in PAX2+ optic disc cells, CNTN2+ axons exited the circular path.
source: In areas where there was a gap in PAX2+ optic disc cells, CNTN2+ axons exited the circular path (diamond arrow in Figure 7A; a gap between two arrowheads in Figure 7B and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, B and F.

claim: In regions where POU4F2+ RGCs were a few hundred micrometers away from PAX2+ optic disc cells, RGCs grew axons in centrifugal directions.
source: In regions where POU4F2+ RGCs were a few hundred micrometers away from PAX2+ optic disc cells, RGCs grew axons in centrifugal directions (arrow in Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Very similar findings were found using hiPSCs, indicating the reproducibility of CONCEPT organoids in multiple cell lines.
source: Very similar findings were found using hiPSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), indicating the reproducibility of CONCEPT organoids in multiple cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAX2+ optic disc cells did not express ALDH1A3; instead, the path for RGC axon growth was bordered by two cell populations that highly expressed ALDH1A3.
source: PAX2+ optic disc cells did not express ALDH1A3; instead, the path for RGC axon growth was bordered by two cell populations that highly expressed ALDH1A3 (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: In mice, Aldh1a3 expression was low in differentiating RGCs in the central retina but high in peripheral retinal progenitors and in the optic stalk.
source: In mice, Aldh1a3 expression was low in differentiating RGCs in the central retina but high in peripheral retinal progenitors (Figure 7K) and in the optic stalk (Li et al., 2000), consistent with ALDH1A3 expression in CONCEPT organoids (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7K and citation to Li et al., 2000.

claim: In mice, Vax1 and Vax2 are expressed in the optic stalk and ventral retina and are jointly required for the optic stalk development.
source: In mice, Vax1 and Vax2 are expressed in the optic stalk and ventral retina and are jointly required for the optic stalk development (Mui et al., 2005; Take-uchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mui et al., 2005; Take-uchi et al., 2003.

claim: In CONCEPT organoids, cells that set up the inner boundary for RGC axon growth also expressed optic-stalk marker VAX1/2.
source: In CONCEPT organoids, cells that set up the inner boundary for RGC axon growth also expressed optic-stalk marker VAX1/2 (Figure 7I and J; the antibody recognizes both VAX1 and VAX2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7I and J.

claim: Immunostaining of CONCEPT organoids confirms that CNTN2 is a specific cell-surface marker for differentiating human RGCs.
source: Taken together, immunostaining of CONCEPT organoids confirms that CNTN2 is a specific cell-surface marker for differentiating human RGCs
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining data shown in Figure 7.

claim: RGCs grow axons toward and then along a path that is defined by adjacent optic disc cells (PAX2+ VSX2+ ALDH1A3-).
source: RGCs grow axons toward and then along a path that is defined by adjacent optic disc cells (PAX2+ VSX2+ ALDH1A3-).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial organization and marker expression patterns shown in Figure 7.

claim: From 100 retinal organoids on days 41–48, around 385,000 RGCs were isolated.
source: From 100 retinal organoids on days 41–48, around 385,000 RGCs were isolated.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from MACS isolation.

claim: Isolated RGCs exhibited neuronal morphology and widely expressed RGC markers TUBB3 and POU4F2.
source: These cells exhibited neuronal morphology and widely expressed RGC markers TUBB3 and POU4F2 (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: In contrast to directional axon growth found in CONCEPT organoids, isolated RGCs grew neurites in random directions.
source: In contrast to directional axon growth found in CONCEPT organoids, isolated RGCs grew neurites in random directions (Figure 7L), indicating the differences in axon pathfinding cues between CONCEPT organoids and purified RGC cultures.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7L and inference about differences in culture conditions.

claim: A portion of isolated RGCs expressed POU4F2 but not CNTN2, indicating that CNTN2 was downregulated in dissociated RGC cultures.
source: A portion of isolated RGCs expressed POU4F2 but not CNTN2 (Figure 7M), indicating that CNTN2 was downregulated in dissociated RGC cultures.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7M and inference from marker expression patterns.

claim: Isolated RGCs also expressed RGC markers ISL1, RBPMS, and SNCG.
source: Isolated RGCs also expressed RGC markers ISL1, RBPMS, and SNCG (Figure 7N–P).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7N-P.

claim: RGCs displayed a hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (mean ± SD: –20.1±6.4 mV).
source: Using current-clamp configuration, we found that RGCs displayed a hyperpolarized resting membrane potential (mean ± SD: –20.1±6.4 mV, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: When cells were held at –70 mV by current injection, in most cases (6/9), depolarizing currents steps could trigger an action potential.
source: When cells were held at –70 mV by current injection, in most cases (6/9), depolarizing currents steps could trigger an action potential, which was followed by a depolarization plateau if the current was injected for more than 10ms (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: From a holding membrane potential of –80 mV, both inward and outward currents (Im) were observed in response to depolarizing voltage steps (Vm).
source: From a holding membrane potential of –80 mV, both inward and outward currents (Im) were observed in response to depolarizing voltage steps (Vm, Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Outward currents were primarily mediated by voltage-gated potassium channels, as application of 20 mM TEA significantly reduced their amplitude.
source: Outward currents were primarily mediated by voltage-gated potassium channels, as application of 20 mM TEA significantly reduced their amplitude (mean IK ± SD at 60 mV; 964±537 pA in control; 279±201 pA in TEA, U=24.0; p=0.019, two-sided MannWhitneyU test, Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8D with statistical analysis.

claim: 1 µM TTX abolished all inward currents, demonstrating that they were mediated by activation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: Conversely, 1 µM TTX abolished all inward currents, demonstrating that they were mediated by activation of voltage-gated sodium channels (mean INa ± SD at –10 mV; –338.2±121 in control; –18.3±13 pA in TTX; U=0.0; p=0.035, two-sided MannWhitneyU test, Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8E with statistical analysis.

claim: Isolated RGCs exhibit functional features traditionally found in excitable cells, such as in neurons.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that isolated RGCs exhibit functional features traditionally found in excitable cells, such as in neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8.

claim: FGF8 and FGF9 were differentially expressed in PAX2+ optic disc cells of CONCEPT organoids.
source: To assess the roles of FGF8 and FGF9 in CONCEPT organoids, we validated that FGF8 and FGF9 were differentially expressed in PAX2+ optic disc cells of CONCEPT organoids (Figure 9B–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9B-E.

claim: TUBB3+ RGC axons grew towards and then along the regions with high-level FGF8 and FGF9 expression.
source: TUBB3+ RGC axons grew towards and then along the regions with high-level FGF8 and FGF9 expression (Figure 9D and E), suggesting that FGF8 and FGF9 may attract RGC axon growth.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and E and speculation about their role.

claim: FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3, MAP2K1, and MAP2K2 were expressed in multiple types of cells in CONCEPT organoids.
source: Additionally, FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3, MAP2K1, and MAP2K2 were expressed in multiple types of cells in CONCEPT organoids.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: In RGCs, FGFR1 and MAP2K2 were clearly expressed.
source: In RGCs, FGFR1 and MAP2K2 were clearly expressed (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), indicating that RGCs expressed the components that transduce the signals from FGF ligands.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and inference about signaling.

claim: After the FGFR inhibition, FGF8 expression was grossly unaffected.
source: After the FGFR inhibition, FGF8 expression was grossly unaffected.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 9.

claim: Despite persistent FGF8, the number of RGC somas were drastically reduced after FGFR inhibition.
source: Despite persistent FGF8, the number of RGC somas were drastically reduced (Figure 9F–K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9F-K.

claim: After FGFR inhibition, remaining RGCs nearly did not grow directional axons.
source: Notably, remaining RGCs nearly did not grow directional axons (arrowheads in Figure 9K), and a few remaining axons wandered around (arrow in Figure 9K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9K.

claim: FGF signaling mediated by FGFRs is required for early RGC differentiation and directional axon growth in human cells.
source: These findings indicate that (a) PAX2+ optic disc cells differentially expressed FGF8 and FGF9; (b) FGF signaling mediated by FGFRs is required for early RGC differentiation and directional axon growth in human cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the FGFR inhibition experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: In chicks, FGF8 and FGF3 coordinate the initiation of retinal differentiation.
source: In chicks, FGF8 and FGF3 coordinate the initiation of retinal differentiation Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Vogel-Höpker et al., 2000
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Vogel-Höpker et al., 2000.

claim: FGF8 maintains PAX2 expression in optic nerve explants.
source: FGF8 maintains PAX2 expression in optic nerve explants (Soukkarieh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soukkarieh et al., 2007.

claim: In mice, FGF8 and FGF9 trigger axon outgrowth in motor neuron column explants.
source: In mice, FGF8 and FGF9 trigger axon outgrowth in motor neuron column explants (Shirasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shirasaki et al., 2006.

claim: Cysts mimic the anterior ectoderm in the epithelial structure and cell fates.
source: Collectively, cysts mimic the anterior ectoderm in the epithelial structure and cell fates.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and discussion.

claim: Individual cysts efficiently generate telencephalic and ocular tissues in the absence of any extrinsic factors, indicating their default cell fates of the anterior ectoderm.
source: In this study, individual cysts efficiently generate telencephalic and ocular tissues in the absence of any extrinsic factors, indicating their default cell fates of the anterior ectoderm.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference about cell fate.

claim: Epiblast cells are epigenetically primed for ectodermal fates.
source: Our findings are consistent with the reports that epiblast cells are epigenetically primed for ectodermal fates (Argelaguet et al., 2019) and neuroectodermal tissues are the default differentiation from pluripotent stem cells (Muñoz-Sanjuán and Brivanlou, 2002; Tropepe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Argelaguet et al., 2019; Muñoz-Sanjuán and Brivanlou, 2002; Tropepe et al., 2001.

claim: Neuroectodermal tissues are the default differentiation from pluripotent stem cells.
source: Our findings are consistent with the reports that epiblast cells are epigenetically primed for ectodermal fates (Argelaguet et al., 2019) and neuroectodermal tissues are the default differentiation from pluripotent stem cells (Muñoz-Sanjuán and Brivanlou, 2002; Tropepe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muñoz-Sanjuán and Brivanlou, 2002; Tropepe et al., 2001.

claim: In CONCEPT organoids on days 22–26, FOXG1+ telencephalon, PAX2+ VSX2- optic stalk, PAX2+ VSX2+ optic disc, and VSX2+ neuroretinal tissues are positioned along the center-periphery axis, mimicking the sequence of their spatial positions in E13.5 mouse embryos.
source: In CONCEPT organoids on days 22–26, FOXG1+ telencephalon, PAX2+ VSX2- optic stalk, PAX2+ VSX2+ optic disc, and VSX2+ neuroretinal tissues are positioned along the center-periphery axis, mimicking the sequence of their spatial positions in E13.5 mouse embryos.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and comparison with in vivo development.

claim: The formation of telencephalic and retinal tissues are highly coordinated, consistent with the prosomere model.
source: Our findings indicate that the formation of telencephalic and retinal tissues are highly coordinated, consistent with the prosomere model (Martínez-Morales et al., 2004; Redies and Puelles, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations and supported by citations to Martínez-Morales et al., 2004; Redies and Puelles, 2001.

claim: The tissue patterning in CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids is originated from the attachment of a radially-symmetric epithelium to the culture surface for growth as colonies.
source: The tissue patterning in CONCEPT telencephalon-eye organoids is originated from the attachment of a radially-symmetric epithelium to the culture surface for growth as colonies since individual cysts kept in suspensions do not form any apparent tissue patterning.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations and comparison of different culture conditions.

claim: Timed BMP4 treatment is shown to promote neuroretinal differentiation from pluripotent stem cells.
source: In literature, timed BMP4 treatment is shown to promote neuroretinal differentiation from pluripotent stem cells (Kuwahara et al., 2015), and FGF8 promotes telencephalic and eye development (Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Wilson and Rubenstein, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuwahara et al., 2015; Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Wilson and Rubenstein, 2000.

claim: FGF8 promotes telencephalic and eye development.
source: In literature, timed BMP4 treatment is shown to promote neuroretinal differentiation from pluripotent stem cells (Kuwahara et al., 2015), and FGF8 promotes telencephalic and eye development (Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Wilson and Rubenstein, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2005; Wilson and Rubenstein, 2000.

claim: In the mouse retina, multiple RGC axon guidance cues are concentrically organized around the optic disc, regulating RGC axon growth and exit from the eye through the optic stalk.
source: In the mouse retina, multiple RGC axon guidance cues are concentrically organized around the optic disc, regulating RGC axon growth and exit from the eye through the optic stalk (Oster et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oster et al., 2004.

claim: It is accepted that the optic-disc regions provide growth-promoting guidance cues, whereas peripheral retinal regions provide inhibitory guidance cues.
source: It is accepted that the optic-disc regions provide growth-promoting guidance cues, whereas peripheral retinal regions provide inhibitory guidance cues (Oster et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oster et al., 2004.
